sources.note: Only book-length phonology of the Saparua language of which Latu is (per Collins 1983, Kotynski 1989) the most divergent dialect; a Pusat Bahasa-style phonology normally has a 'tekanan' section. Would give a related-variety (sapa1251) statement, not Latu itself.

sources.citation: Erniati. 2016. Distribusi fonem bahasa di Pulau Saparua: data Negeri Sirisori Islam. Totobuang 4(1): 27-39. Ambon: Kantor Bahasa Maluku. DOI 10.26499/ttbng.v4i1.3
sources.note: Related variety only (Sirisori Islam dialect of Saparua, on Saparua Island; not Latu). Segmental inventory (6 V, 17 C). Stress appears only as an allophonic environment: '[E], terjadi pada suku terbuka yang mendapat tekanan' / '[O], terjadi pada suku terbuka yang mendapat tekanan' (pp. 34-35); no statement of where stress falls.

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: ANU. x+177 pp.
sources.note: Latu appears ~40 times as comparative data ('Latu (a Saparua language spoken on the west shore of Elpaputi Bay, Seram)', ch. on PAN *e; fn. 6: Saparua 'survives . the villages of Tumalehu, Hualoi and Latu at the mouth of Elpaputi Bay'). Every stress statement concerns other languages: 'Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word' (pp. 82-83); Kaibobo 'e when stressed, o when unstressed' (fn. 87-88); Tehoru, Buru. Sile…

sources.citation: Ekris, A. van. 1864-1865. Woordenlijst van eenige dialecten der landtaal op de Ambonsche eilanden. Mededeelingen van wege het Nederlandsche Zendelinggenootschap 8: 61-108, 301-336; 9: 109-136. Rotterdam.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone; the introduction discusses only spelling (b~w and d~l alternation in the 'Alfoersch' dialect, l~r elsewhere, u for the oe sound). Van Hoevell 1877:13 quotes van Ekris's 'toelichting' on the articulation of the Saparua/Nusalaut -nno/-llo/-njo/-ljo endings (held consonant, very short final -no/-jo), which is the nearest thing to a prosodic remark.
No descriptive references; only Collins 1983 and Edwards & Grimes 2021 (subclassification commentary).

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 2018. Penelitian Bahasa di Maluku. Ambon: Kantor Bahasa Maluku, Badan Pengembangan dan Pembinaan Bahasa, Kementerian Pendidikan dan Kebudayaan. xiv+190 pp. (preface signed James T. Collins, 10 Februari 2018; ISBN field blank in the online PDF; in Indonesian).
sources.note: Nothing on Latu (or Saparua) stress or tone. Latu content: p. 52 'dalam dialek tertentu /-lo/ yang sudah menjadi sufiks fosil ini memengaruhi vokal dan konsonan sebelumnya.. misalnya sebutan dalam varian Saparua di Desa Latu, Seram' (fossilised article **lo colouring the preceding V and C), the shared Saparua/Nusalaut innovation *p > /h/ or zero, 1970s vitality ('bahasa Saparua bertahan; begitu juga di Latu, Tumalehu, dan Hualoi', p. 53) and p. 90 'Latu, Tumalehu, dan Hualoi, suatu dialek Saparua dituturkan'. The book's only word-stress ('tekanan') passages concern other languages: Luhu, pp.…

sources.citation: Holton, Gary. 1996. Bibliography of language and language use in North and Central Maluku. Southeast Asia Paper no. 40. Honolulu: Center for Southeast Asian Studies, School of Hawaiian, Asian and Pacific Studies, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. 115 pp.
sources.note: no phonology content (bibliography); used as a pointer list -- it led to van Hoevell 1877 (work 1) and confirms that up to 1996 no phonology or grammar of Latu or of Saparua existed apart from van Hoevell's 1877 sketch, Stresemann 1927 and Collins's unpublished 1970s field notes.

sources.citation: Kotynski, Edward A. 1989. A lexicostatistic survey of the Lease islands. In Wyn D. Laidig (ed.), Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 6: Maluku, 1-14. Ambon: Pattimura University / SIL.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Latu wordlist taken 4/10/85 from Abdul Latip Patty (age 20, reliability 'good', by E. Leslie). p. 8: 'The Latu (Seram) dialect which is also spoken in Hualoi and Tumalehu, Seram, (Collins 1983), is the most divergent dialect of the Saparua language, scoring as a different language in the reduced matrix.. it is counted as a dialect of Saparua in this study.' Latu village pop. 2134, Islam.

sources.citation: Taguchi, Yushin. 1989. Lexicostatistic survey of the languages indigenous to West Seram. In Wyn D. Laidig (ed.), Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 6: Maluku, 15-63. Ambon: Pattimura University / SIL.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 4.3.1.11 SAPARUA: 'spoken in eight villages: five villages on Seram (Iha, Kulur, Latu, Hualoy and Tumalehu) and three villages on Saparua (Iha, Kulur and Siri-Sori Islam).. The language is also spoken by some Latu people living in Kairatu village.' Lexicostatistics only (whole volume: zero hits for stress/accent/tekanan).

sources.citation: Collins, James T. 1982. Prothesis in the languages of Central Maluku: an argument from Proto-Austronesian grammar. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 2: Tracking the travellers, 187-200. Pacific Linguistics C-75. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.note: Historical phonology and morphology only: Latu h- < PCM *b-initial nouns after loss of *k (hahil 'hook', haho 'thread', hahune 'dove'), zero vs Sepa-Teluti y- prothesis, retention of PAN *si, glottal stop in Latu forms ([a?aheto], na?i), reduplicative instrumental nominalisation. The only occurrence of 'stress' is syntactic ('used to stress the readers or patient', p. 191). No statement on word stress, accent or tone; no stress marks on the Latu forms.
